items.rationale: It is a workflow: the order of the calls is written in the code, and the model's output only fills in the slot values. Using a model, its output, or tools does not hand it the control flow; a or c shows that mix-up.

accepted: the model decides, so an agent
items.rationale: It is an agent: each pass the model decides whether to call a tool or finish, so the model owns the control flow, and the code only runs the loop and the tools. Answering workflow because Python wrote a for loop shows M17.

The path is known and the format never changes, so a fixed workflow gives one pass, a steady cost and testable output. Choosing an agent for flexibility or self-checking nobody needs shows M11; claiming an agent could not do the summary treats the workflow as the only way a model can be used, which is not true of either design.
The agent costs 6 x $0.003 x 1,000 = $18 and the workflow 2 x $0.003 x 1,000 = $6, so the difference is $12. An answer of 18 or 6 gives one design's total instead of the difference.

Job A has known steps and needs the same checks and an audit trail, so a workflow fits; Job B needs a variable number of lookups, so a model-driven loop with the 8-call cap fits. Using workflows or one agent for everything shows M14 or M11, and reversing the roles shows M15.

In the final stage the model's output picks the next step and when to stop, so that stage is an agent loop inside an otherwise code-driven workflow. Classify, retrieve and draft run in the order the code sets; naming classify shows M10, the idea that any model decision gives it control.
